consensus: KV cache compression is about reducing the memory footprint of attention state during long-context inference.
The cache grows linearly with sequence length, so longer conversations or agent loops can become memory-bound even when model weights fit.
Useful approaches include sharing KV tensors across heads or layers, reducing the precision of stored cache values, or shortening the effective sequence.
The main benefit is lower serving memory pressure, which can improve throughput, concurrency, latency, or cost without retraining the base model in some cases.
The main tradeoff is that every compression method risks some loss of attention fidelity, and methods differ in what they compress and how complex they are to implement.

evidence_quality: Strong agreement across three reviewed sources that KV cache growth is a real serving bottleneck in long-context systems.
Evidence is conceptually strong but operationally general: the sources explain the mechanism and tradeoffs, but do not provide workload-specific benchmarks here.
Several claims are review or synthesis claims rather than primary experimental results, so this page is best for orientation and design framing.
Confidence is highest on the memory-scaling problem and the existence of multiple compression levers; it is lower on which method is best in any specific deployment.
executive_synthesis: KV cache compression matters when long-context serving starts to hit memory limits. The KV cache is the runtime store of attention state, and it grows with sequence length, so it can become the dominant GPU memory consumer even when the model itself is small enough to fit. In practice, KV cache compression is an infrastructure lever for keeping more context active, or serving more concurrent sessions, without retraining the model. The main mechanisms are to share KV states across heads or layers, store cache values at lower precision, or compress the sequence itself. The caveat is that each option trades away something: attention fidelity, model capacity, or implementation simplicity. The evidence is consistent on the problem and the broad solution space, but thin on exact production guidance, so this is a design-and-triage topic rather than a one-size-fits-all recipe.

practical_example.example: A team runs a retrieval-heavy assistant for internal support. Users often keep long threads open, and each new turn increases the KV cache. The system starts to cap concurrency because GPU memory fills up before compute does. Instead of retraining the model, the team tests a cache compression approach that reduces per-token storage or shares cache state more aggressively. They validate it on the same hardware and traffic patterns they use in production, because a method that looks good in isolation can still hurt response quality or fail to fit the real serving stack.

practical_example.why_it_helps: This shows why KV cache compression is usually an operations decision, not just a model-design choice. It connects the abstract idea to a concrete serving bottleneck: memory pressure from long sessions.

practical_takeaway: Treat KV cache size as a first-class serving constraint. If long-context workloads are memory-bound, compare compression methods by what they reduce: per-head cache size, per-layer duplication, or sequence length. Then test on the exact workload and hardware, because the quality and integration risk depend on the method and deployment context.
tensions: Training-free, drop-in methods are attractive because they reduce integration risk, but the evidence does not say they are always the best choice.
Different compression schemes reduce different parts of the problem, so a method that helps memory may not address attention cost in the same way.
The sources agree that quality can degrade, but they do not resolve how much quality loss is acceptable for a given product or workload.
There is no workload-specific benchmark here, so the practical winner remains context dependent.
title: KV Cache Compression
what_to_remember: The KV cache is runtime attention memory, not model weights.
It grows linearly with sequence length, so long contexts can become memory-bound.
Compression can lower memory traffic and serving cost without changing the base model.
Different methods trade off memory savings, fidelity, and implementation complexity.
Do not choose a method without testing it on the real workload and hardware.
